content: Enterobacter is a genus of bacteria that are Gram-negative, rod-shaped, and capable of facultative anaerobic growth. These bacteria belong to the family Enterobacteriaceae. Certain strains of Enterobacter are pathogenic and can cause opportunistic infections, particularly in individuals with compromised immune systems, such as hospitalized patients. The most common sites of infection caused by Enterobacter are the urinary tract and the respiratory tract. Enterobacter can be differentiated from other Gram-negative rods by its ability to rapidly ferment lactose, a characteristic it shares with Escherichia coli and Klebsiella. Two clinically significant species within this genus are Enterobacter aerogenes and Enterobacter cloacae. Antimicrobial Therapy for Enterobacter Infections 1. Empiric Antimicrobial Therapy (Before In Vitro Susceptibility Results Are Available) 1. For non–life-threatening infections or when the prevalence of multidrug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria (MDR-GNB) is less than 20%: Preferred regimen: Piperacillin-Tazobactam 3.375 g administered intravenously every 6 hours, with or without the addition of aminoglycosides. Alternative regimen: Ciprofloxacin 400 mg administered intravenously every 8–12 hours. 2. For life-threatening infections or when the prevalence of MDR-GNB is greater than 20%: Preferred regimen: Meropenem 0.5–1 g administered intravenously every 8 hours. Alternative regimens: 1. Colistin combined with Meropenem 0.5–1 g intravenously every 8 hours. 2. Colistin combined with Imipenem 500 mg intravenously every 6 hours. 3. Colistin combined with Doripenem 500 mg intravenously every 8 hours. 4. Colistin combined with Ertapenem 1 g intravenously every 24 hours. 5. Colistin combined with Fosfomycin 6 g intravenously every 6 hours. 2. Antimicrobial Therapy Based on In Vitro Susceptibility Results 1. If the organism is susceptible to all tested agents: Preferred regimen: Piperacillin-Tazobactam 3.375 g administered intravenously every 6 hours. Alternative regimens: 1. Ciprofloxacin 400 mg administered intravenously every 8–12 hours. 2. Cefepime 2 g administered intravenously every 8 hours (if the minimum inhibitory concentration [MIC] is ≤ 1 μg/mL). 2. If the organism is an extended-spectrum beta-lactamase (ESBL)-producing strain: Preferred regimen: Meropenem 0.5–1 g administered intravenously every 8 hours. Alternative regimens: 1. Imipenem 500 mg administered intravenously every 6 hours. 2. Doripenem 500 mg administered intravenously every 8 hours. 3. Ertapenem 1 g administered intravenously every 24 hours. 4. Cefepime 2 g administered intravenously every 8 hours (if the MIC is ≤ 1 μg/mL). 3. If the organism is resistant to all tested agents: Preferred regimen: Colistin combined with Meropenem 0.5–1 g administered intravenously every 8 hours. Alternative regimens: 1. Colistin combined with Imipenem 500 mg administered intravenously every 6 hours. 2. Colistin combined with Doripenem 500 mg administered intravenously every 8 hours. 3. Colistin combined with Ertapenem 1 g administered intravenously every 24 hours. 4. Colistin combined with Minocycline 100 mg administered intravenously every 12 hours.
